title: Ganapati comes to the street
hookLine: a clay Ganesha carried home under a cloth, and how the god every Hindu begins with went out into the street
carry: ganapati: lord of the ganas, first for everyone
last: JANMASHTAMI: THE INFINITE, SMALL ENOUGH TO HOLD.

lines: A GUEST FOR A FEW DAYS.
cards: In Maharashtra, in late summer, you'll see a family walking home from the market carrying a Ganesha about the size of a toddler, his face covered with a cloth. A cousin is banging a drum.
The kids are shouting Ganpati Bappa Morya. He's made of clay, still slightly damp. At home, a corner has been cleared, a little platform set up, flowers ready.
They'll uncover his face only once he's in his seat. Down the road, a whole neighborhood is putting up a pavilion for a Ganesha three times as tall. Today, the arrival.

teach.b: Chaturthi means the fourth day, the fourth of the bright half of the month of Bhadrapada, in August or September, the day Ganesha is said to have been born.
Remember day twenty-four: Shiva gives the boy an elephant's head, makes him leader of the ganas, his band of followers, and promises he'll be worshipped first. That's his name.

Gana-pati: lord of the ganas, the hosts, the crowd. And the promise holds in a way few gods share: Hindus of almost every tradition, whether they mainly love Shiva, Vishnu or the Goddess, begin with Ganesha.
Now a story from history. For a long time Ganesh Chaturthi was kept mostly at home.
Then in 1893, in Pune, the freedom fighter Bal Gangadhar Tilak helped turn it into a great public festival.

Ganeshas went up in the street, in pavilions put up by whole neighborhoods, with music and speeches, and people came from every lane of the city, under British rule, to gather around a god they all shared.

teach.h: INVITED IN, AND TREATED AS PRESENT.
teach.b: At home, the image is invited in with prana pratishtha, setting the breath in, and from then on he's treated as present: flowers, blades of durva grass, modak, the sweet dumplings in his hand, and arti morning and evening.
Ganapati is the god of the crowd: the one every Hindu home begins with, and so the one a whole street can welcome together. And like any guest, he only stays a while. Tomorrow, the leaving.

how: On Ganesh Chaturthi many Hindus bring a clay image of Ganesha home or to a neighborhood pavilion, invite his presence with prana pratishtha, and honor him daily with flowers, durva grass, modak and arti for one and a half to ten days.

games.q: it's 1893 in Pune, and Tilak wants a festival a whole city can share. which god goes out into the street?
o: Ganapati, the one every home begins with.
a brand-new god made up for the occasion.
games.why: Ganapati, lord of the ganas. almost every Hindu tradition starts with him, so whole neighborhoods could welcome him together.

practice: Picture Ganesha carried through your front door, face covered, drums behind him. Clear a spot for him, set him on a small cloth, lift the cloth from his face, and offer something first: a flower, a sweet, a few blades of grass.
If you pray, say the short mantra many begin with: Om Gam Ganapataye Namah. If you don't, just sit with him a while, like a guest who's just arrived.
